France to Italy, cost-of-living protests rock EU: Stores looted, 140-year-old landmark set on fire

Demonstrations come at a politically consequential moment for Europe, amid an unprecedented super-cycle of national elections over the next 12 months in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.

Debdutta Chakraborty

18 October, 2026 05:45 pm IST

New Delhi: The streets of several European Union countries saw clashes between security forces and protesters Saturday as thousands took part in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations against the rising cost of living in France, Italy, Belgium and Portugal. In France, where 1,200 people were arrested, the unrest involved clashes, looting, fires and damage to public buildings and businesses. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the “violence of extreme intensity”.

The demonstrations come at a politically consequential moment for Europe, amid an unprecedented super-cycle of national elections over the next 12 months, with polls scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.

Show Full Article

France sees most turbulent protests in decades France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to its Interior Ministry. Police confronted protesters across the country as some gatherings descended into clashes, looting and arson.

Prime Minister Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers injured, according to French newspaper Le Monde . Dozens of shops, including those of the country’s famous fashion brands like Louis Vuitton and Hermès, were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, AFP reported. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said entire streets in the capital “have been devastated”.

In Limoges, a fire set by masked protesters largely destroyed the town hall, a building more than 140 years old. City halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised, while protesters in Lyon set fire to the city’s tourist office.

As the protests, which began last month, escalated into widespread violence, President Emmanuel Macron said those responsible for attacking public buildings and businesses and for looting would be “prosecuted and punished”.

Aucune place pour la violence dans notre République.

Ceux qui ont cassé, attaqué les préfectures comme les commerces, pillé jusqu’à nos mairies, seront poursuivis et punis.

Aux forces de l’ordre, garantes du droit à manifester, je dis le soutien de la Nation.

Nous ferons tous…

— Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) October 17, 2026

“No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished… We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he wrote on X.

Meloni asks Opposition to condemn violence In Italy, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in central Milan Saturday. The march, organised around opposition to wars and rising living costs, began peacefully. However, masked protesters later threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables, according to local reports.

Police deployed water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds. At least two police personnel were injured, and about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, detained, according to Italian news agency LaPresse .

Responding to the protests, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X, “Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not.” While acknowledging the role of protests in a healthy democracy, she blamed “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and hold entire cities hostage”.

Ho grande rispetto per le migliaia di persone che oggi hanno manifestato pacificamente, anche partecipando alla mobilitazione indetta dalla CGIL che ha visto anche la partecipazione dei leader della sinistra. Qualunque siano le idee per le quali si manifesta, la partecipazione è… pic.twitter.com/nZn0emcGrq

— Giorgia Meloni (@GiorgiaMeloni) October 17, 2026

Meloni also urged Opposition parties to unequivocally condemn the violence and call for peaceful demonstrations.

Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, acknowledged the grievances behind the protests while condemning the violence. “The reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable,” he said.

In Brussels, Belgium, police fired tear gas and deployed water cannons as hundreds took to the streets, and allegedly threw projectiles at officers and set fires. The demonstrations followed weeks of student protests over high university registration fees, adding education-related grievances to wider discontent over living costs.

In Lisbon, Portugal, thousands marched Saturday against the rising cost of living, low wages and the growing difficulty of securing housing in major cities. The march followed days of build-up.

Portugal’s Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said the government would not give in to the demonstrations. “The government will not yield to shouts from the street,” he was quoted as saying on Friday.

How France became centre of protests The protests in France began last month at high schools in the suburbs of Paris over teacher shortages and inadequate facilities. They spread to other parts of Paris and then nationwide, growing into a broader agitation over the high cost of living.

The protests have also attracted international attention. Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump blamed the unrest on Islam and migration. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out-of-control mass migration,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding, “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country!”

Saturday’s protests also echoed the 2018 “yellow vest” movement against the Macron government over rising fuel prices and the cost of living. AP reported that protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the movement, with many wearing the fluorescent yellow vests that became a symbol of the 2018 rallies.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)

France counts cost of worst unrest in years

By Sybille de La Hamaide PARIS, Oct 18 (Reuters) – France woke on Sunday to the wreckage of one of its most violent days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, hundreds of police injured and nearly 1,800 people arrested.

Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.

One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, where police made a record 855 arrests. Across France, more than 500 officers were injured, the interior minister said.

Show Full Article

“It’s like a war zone here,” said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, which suffered major damage on Saturday.

More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.

President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 2000 local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said.

SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED

While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.

A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday.

In Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and spray-painted slogans bore witness to a day that began largely with peaceful demonstrations but descended into violence.

In Limoges, southwestern France, mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city’s 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and partially destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris’s Notre-Dame Cathedral.

“There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives,” Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the million euros needed to repair the city hall.

The unrest has increased pressure on President Macron and his government, with a presidential election due next year. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.

Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. “Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” Lescure said in a statement.

Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses impacted by the violence.

French retailer Carrefour’s Chief Executive Alexandre Bompard told BFMTV that 50 of the company’s shops had been damaged including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the dozens of millions of euros.

The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.

(Reporting by Sybille de La Hamaide; editing by Richard Lough and Elaine Hardcastle)

By Joshua McElwee VATICAN CITY, Oct 18 (Reuters) – Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter’s Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.

The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.

Smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.

Show Full Article

“Having overcome this delicate phase … I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” Leo said.

The pope, who was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.

He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”.

(Reporting by Joshua McElwee;Editing by Sara Rossi and Helen Popper)
